implementation_notes: The dominant JVM realization is an auditing framework rather than a hand-written collection: annotate the entity (or just the properties that need history) with @Audited and Envers writes an entity_table_AUD audit table per revision; AuditReader, obtained from AuditReaderFactory, answers the pattern's questions - getRevisionNumberForDate(LocalDateTime) turns a date into the revision current at that instant, find(Entity.class, id, rev) / createQuery().forEntitiesAtRevision(...) read the entity as it was, forRevisionsOfEntity lists the changes, and AuditEntity.property("salary").hasChanged() filters the revisions that touched one property. What replaces the classic structure: revision numbering, the AUD tables and the as-of read; the domain class keeps ordinary getters. Keep a hand-written temporal collection when the index is business (valid) time, when the property must be read without a persistence context, or when the store is not JPA.
pitfalls: Audit queries are much slower than live queries (correlated subselects) and the AUD tables grow without bound: index the revision columns, partition or prune, and never use the audit path for hot reads.

Envers records transaction time (global revision + commit timestamp), not business validity: a back-dated correction is visible as a new revision, not as the value that was in force last quarter - that needs the entity's own valid-from column.

A part-audited entity produces partially historical objects: non-audited fields carry their current value in an as-of read, so mixing audited and non-audited state in one domain object is a silent correctness bug.
LocalDate/LocalDateTime have no zone: converting a stored UTC instant with the JVM default zone (or vice versa) shifts the as-of date, so the conversion zone must be explicit.

variants.name: hand-written temporal collection (Fowler's original)
variants.implementation_notes: Fowler's original Java realization: a temporal collection held as a NavigableMap keyed by effective date, with get(LocalDate) returning floorEntry(when), a no-argument get() defaulting to an injected Clock's today, and put(from, value) appending a version. java.time.LocalDate is the Time Point and the map's ordering makes milestones() a descendingMap() traversal; a bi-temporal collection is simply a temporal collection whose values are temporal collections. Choose it when the index is business validity, when the history must be read without a persistence context, or when the store is not JPA - the classic form is also the only one that can hold a value valid over two disjoint ranges.
pitfalls: LocalDate.now() / Instant.now() without an injected Clock makes tests and replays non-deterministic and hides the zone (LocalDate.now() uses the JVM default zone) - inject the clock, as above.

floorEntry returns null before the first milestone and TreeMap.put at an existing key silently replaces the version, so same-date updates and range-splitting corrections need entry-level keys or a second dimension.
A TreeMap cannot store null values in a meaningful way: a null lookup result is indistinguishable from an absent key, so a legitimate null value must be wrapped.

The map is not thread-safe: concurrent put/get need external synchronisation, a ConcurrentSkipListMap, or the collection must be confined to one thread - and a ConcurrentSkipListMap has no floorEntry/floorKey combination plus atomic update, so the read-then-write of a retroactive range rewrite is still not atomic.
